title: Time Until Next Customer Event Using LEAD
description:
For each customer event show the next event date and the number of days until that next event (within the same customer).

**Table: customer_events** — `customer_id`, `event_date`, `event_type`

Output columns: `customer_id`, `event_date`, `event_type`, `next_event_date`, `days_until_next`. Order by `customer_id`, `event_date`.
schema_sql: CREATE TABLE customer_events (customer_id INT, event_date DATE, event_type VARCHAR); INSERT INTO customer_events VALUES (1,'2026-01-05','login'),(1,'2026-01-12','purchase'),(1,'2026-02-01','login'),(1,'2026-02-15','review'),(2,'2026-01-08','login'),(2,'2026-01-20','purchase'),(2,'2026-02-10','login');
solution_sql: SELECT customer_id, event_date, event_type, LEAD(event_date) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY event_date) AS next_event_date, LEAD(event_date) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY event_date) - event_date AS days_until_next FROM customer_events ORDER BY customer_id, event_date

test_cases.description: 7 events for 2 customers; last event per customer has NULL next_event_date

hints: LEAD(event_date) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY event_date) gets the next event date within the same customer's history.
The last event per customer returns NULL for next_event_date since there is no following row in the partition.
explanation: LEAD() is the forward-looking counterpart to LAG(). PARTITION BY customer_id ensures we only look ahead within the same customer's events. Subtracting dates gives the interval in days. Customer 1: login→purchase (7 days), purchase→login (20 days), login→review (14 days), review→NULL. Customer 2: login→purchase (12 days), purchase→login (21 days), login→NULL.
